[THOUGHT]  
The patient presents with a constellation of systemic “B symptoms” (fever—though denied, night sweats, weight loss >10% body weight or >5 kg), plus fatigue, abdominal pain/fullness (suggesting possible splenomegaly or intra-abdominal lymphadenopathy), and rapidly progressive cervical lymphadenopathy. Laboratory findings show elevated WBC and LDH — both red flags for lymphoproliferative disorders. The excisional biopsy reveals CD20-positive lymphocytes with high proliferative index — strongly indicative of a B-cell lymphoma, most likely aggressive (e.g., diffuse large B-cell lymphoma) given the rapid onset (4-day neck swelling), constitutional symptoms, and elevated LDH. Absence of fever does not exclude lymphoma, as B symptoms may be partial. Further staging workup (e.g., CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, bone marrow biopsy, PET-CT) would be indicated next.

[SUMMARY]  
**Clinical Summary:**  
A patient presents with 4 weeks of progressive fatigue, abdominal pain and early satiety/fullness, unintentional weight loss (5.4 kg / 12 lb), drenching night sweats, and new-onset cervical lymphadenopathy (4 days). No fever, cough, dyspnea, rash, pruritus, or bruising reported.  

**Key Diagnostic Findings:**  
- CBC: Elevated white blood cell count, mildly decreased hemoglobin, normal platelets  
- LDH: Elevated  
- Cervical lymph node excisional biopsy: CD20-positive lymphocytes with high proliferative index  

**Impression:**  
Highly suggestive of **CD20-positive B-cell lymphoma**, most consistent with **diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL)** given aggressive clinical presentation (rapid lymphadenopathy, B symptoms, elevated LDH, cytopenia).  

**Next Steps (Implied):**  
- Staging imaging: Contrast-enhanced CT (chest/abdomen/pelvis) or PET-CT  
- Bone marrow biopsy and aspiration  
- Flow cytometry and molecular studies on biopsy tissue (e.g., MYC, BCL2, BCL6 FISH)  
- Assessment of HIV status and hepatitis B/C serologies (per standard lymphoma workup)  
- Referral to hematologic oncology for definitive diagnosis and treatment planning  

No other lab/imaging results (CMP, uric acid, CXR, neck US) were provided in this dialogue segment.

[THOUGHT]  
The clinical presentation is classic for systemic B-cell lymphoma: constitutional “B symptoms” (fever is absent, but drenching night sweats + weight loss >10% body weight would meet criteria — here weight loss is 5.4 kg; though not explicitly stated as >10%, in context of 4-week rapid onset and other B symptoms, it contributes to high suspicion), progressive fatigue, early satiety/abdominal pain (suggestive of splenic or intra-abdominal lymphomatous involvement), new cervical lymphadenopathy, and laboratory abnormalities including leukocytosis (often reactive or lymphomatous), mild anemia (likely marrow infiltration or chronic disease), and elevated LDH (a marker of tumor burden and cell turnover). The excisional biopsy finding of CD20-positive lymphocytes with high proliferative index is definitive evidence of a clonal, aggressive B-cell neoplasm. CD20 positivity confirms B-cell lineage; high Ki-67 (implied by “high proliferative index”) supports aggressiveness. DLBCL is the most common aggressive B-cell lymphoma and the prototypical disease fitting this constellation: rapidly progressive, extranodal symptoms (abdominal pain, early satiety), B symptoms, elevated LDH, cytopenias, and bulky nodal disease. While other CD20+ B-cell lymphomas (e.g., Burkitt lymphoma, mantle cell, high-grade B-cell lymphoma NOS) are possible, DLBCL is by far the most prevalent (~90% of diffuse large B-cell malignancies) and best fits the clinical tempo and morphology implied (no mention of starry-sky histology, blastoid features, or MYC/BCL2 double-hit architecture — those would be specified if present). Importantly, no findings contradict DLBCL: absence of fever does not exclude B symptoms (≥2 of fever, night sweats, weight loss ≥10% in 6 months — here night sweats + weight loss + fatigue + lymphadenopathy strongly support systemic lymphoma); normal platelets argue against advanced marrow replacement but do not exclude early/mid-stage DLBCL; lack of reported CNS symptoms or testicular involvement doesn’t exclude DLBCL — it just means those sites aren’t yet involved or assessed.

[EVIDENCE]  
- 4 weeks of progressive fatigue  
- Abdominal pain and early satiety/fullness  
- Unintentional weight loss (5.4 kg / 12 lb)  
- Drenching night sweats  
- New-onset cervical lymphadenopathy (4 days)  
- Elevated white blood cell count  
- Mildly decreased hemoglobin  
- Normal platelets  
- Elevated LDH  
- Cervical lymph node excisional biopsy shows CD20-positive lymphocytes  
- Cervical lymph node excisional biopsy shows high proliferative index  

[DIFFERENTIAL]  
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL)  
Supporting: 4 weeks of progressive fatigue, abdominal pain and early satiety/fullness, unintentional weight loss, drenching night sweats, new-onset cervical lymphadenopathy, elevated WBC, mildly decreased Hb, elevated LDH, CD20-positive lymphocytes, high proliferative index  
Against: none reported  
Verdict: KEEP  

Burkitt lymphoma  
Supporting: CD20-positive lymphocytes, high proliferative index, elevated LDH, abdominal pain/early satiety (common in ileocecal involvement), rapid lymphadenopathy, B symptoms  
Against: none reported — but note: Burkitt typically shows *extremely* high proliferative index (~100%), starry-sky histology, and frequent MYC translocation; none of these distinguishing features are mentioned (nor excluded — they are simply not specified)  
Verdict: KEEP  

Mantle cell lymphoma (MCL)  
Supporting: CD20-positive lymphocytes, lymphadenopathy, B symptoms (night sweats, weight loss), elevated LDH, cytopenias  
Against: none reported — but MCL often presents with GI polyposis (“lymphomatous polyposis”), leukocytosis less typical (more common: lymphocytosis), and SOX11+ or cyclin D1+ immunophenotype not mentioned; however, absence of these markers is not stated — they are pending/unreported  
Verdict: KEEP  

Follicular lymphoma (grade 3B)  
Supporting: CD20-positive lymphocytes, lymphadenopathy, B symptoms, elevated LDH  
Against: typically indolent tempo — but grade 3B is aggressive and can mimic DLBCL; no histologic description (e.g., follicular architecture) is provided, so cannot confirm or exclude  
Verdict: KEEP  

High-grade B-cell lymphoma, NOS (HGBCL-NOS)  
Supporting: CD20-positive, high proliferative index, aggressive clinical course, elevated LDH, B symptoms  
Against: none reported — definition requires exclusion of DLBCL and double-hit lymphoma; neither is ruled out here (FISH pending)  
Verdict: KEEP  

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL)  
Supporting: CD20-positive lymphocytes, lymphadenopathy, fatigue, weight loss  
Against: high proliferative index (CLL/SLL has very low Ki-67), aggressive 4-week tempo (CLL/SLL is indolent), leukocytosis in CLL is usually *lymphocytosis*, not nonspecific WBC elevation — but WBC is only described as “elevated”, not differential; however, high proliferative index is fundamentally at odds with CLL biology  
Verdict: EXCLUDE — high proliferative index directly contradicts the expected low proliferation rate in CLL/SLL  

Hodgkin lymphoma (classical)  
Supporting: cervical lymphadenopathy, B symptoms (night sweats, weight loss), elevated LDH, fatigue  
Against: CD20-positive *lymphocytes* — in cHL, the malignant Reed-Sternberg cells are CD20-negative in ~70–80% of cases (though ~20–30% may show weak/focal CD20); more critically, the biopsy is described as showing CD20-positive *lymphocytes*, implying a monomorphic infiltrate of B cells — not the sparse RS cells in inflammatory background typical of cHL. The phrase “CD20-positive lymphocytes” (plural, diffusely positive) strongly favors non-Hodgkin over Hodgkin lymphoma.  
Verdict: EXCLUDE — the biopsy description (“CD20-positive lymphocytes”) is inconsistent with the cellular composition of classical Hodgkin lymphoma.

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
